title: Hybrid Quantum–Classical Learning Approaches for Scalable Optimization Beyond NISQ Limitations
journal_or_venue: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science, Communication and Technology (IJARSCT)
abstract_summary: The paper proposes a Hybrid Quantum–Classical Machine Learning Framework (HQC-MLF) that embeds parameterized quantum circuits within classical optimization loops, combined with adaptive ansatz selection, error mitigation, and resource-aware scheduling to address large-scale combinatorial and continuous optimization under NISQ hardware constraints. Experimental NISQ simulations on logistics routing, portfolio optimization, and energy load balancing demonstrate faster convergence, improved solution quality, and reduced circuit depth and energy usage compared to purely classical baselines.
methodology_description: The study proposes a Hybrid Quantum–Classical Machine Learning Framework (HQC-MLF) that integrates classical preprocessing and feature encoding with parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs) evaluated inside a classical optimization loop. The architecture consists of: (1) classical preprocessing/feature-encoding to prepare inputs; (2) an adaptive PQC layer where ansatz depth is dynamically increased on stagnation; (3) a classical optimization engine that updates circuit parameters (using gradient information where available) to minimize an expectation-based cost L(θ)=⟨ψ(θ)|H|ψ(θ)⟩ with ψ(θ)=U(θ)|0⟩; (4) error-mitigation and resource-management including zero-noise extrapolation, measurement-error correction, and resource-aware scheduling to trade off depth and noise; and (5) post-processing/decision module to interpret results. Gradients are computed via the parameter-shift rule; adaptive ansatz control increases depth D_new = D_old + δ on convergence stagnation. Experiments are performed in noisy statevector simulations with depolarizing + readout noise; classical optimizers used include Adam and COBYLA, and shots per circuit are 2048. Benchmark problem domains include combinatorial routing, portfolio (quadratic) optimization, and continuous energy load balancing. Performance is evaluated versus classical baselines, reinforcement-learning baselines, and standard QAOA, using metrics such as iterations-to-converge, approximation ratio/optimization score, circuit-depth efficiency, and estimated energy usage.
experimental_setup: Simulations performed using a noisy statevector simulator. Configuration reported: 8–16 qubits, circuit depth 2–10 layers (average circuit depth: QAOA 8 vs HQC-MLF 6), noise model: depolarizing + readout noise, classical optimizers Adam and COBYLA, shots = 2048, simulator type: statevector with added noise.

experiment_process.overview: Hybrid optimization loop combining classical preprocessing, quantum circuit evaluation, and classical parameter updates.
steps: Classical preprocessing and feature encoding of problem instance (routing, portfolio, or load-balancing formulation).
Encode problem Hamiltonian H corresponding to objective (e.g., QUBO / quadratic form for portfolio).
Construct parameterized quantum circuit U(θ) (PQC) with initial ansatz depth.
Evaluate expectation L(θ) = ⟨ψ(θ)|H|ψ(θ)⟩ on noisy statevector simulator with depolarizing + readout noise, using 2048 shots.
Estimate gradients using parameter-shift rule (when applicable) or use gradient-free optimizer (COBYLA) / Adam.
Update parameters: θ_{t+1} = θ_t - η ∇_θ L(θ_t) (or via chosen optimizer).
Apply error mitigation (zero-noise extrapolation, measurement-error correction) to improve expectation estimates.
Monitor convergence; if stagnation detected, adaptively increase ansatz depth D_new = D_old + δ and continue.
Post-process measurement outcomes to extract candidate classical solutions and compute metrics (approximation ratio, energy usage estimate).

results_summary: In NISQ-noise simulations on three benchmark domains (routing, portfolio optimization, energy load balancing) the proposed HQC-MLF—combining classical preprocessing, adaptive PQCs, error mitigation and resource-aware scheduling—converged faster and produced better optimization/approximation scores than tested classical baselines and a QAOA baseline. Reported benefits include fewer iterations to converge, higher solution quality (approximation scores), reduced average circuit depth, and lower estimated energy usage in the simulated experiments. The authors present these results as evidence that hybrid quantum–classical designs can improve scalability under realistic NISQ constraints, while noting further validation on real hardware and larger qubit counts remains future work.

quantum_advantage_detail: The paper reports improved performance of HQC-MLF over classical baselines and QAOA in noise-inclusive simulations, but does not demonstrate hardware-level, large-scale, or provable quantum advantage. The authors frame these simulation results as a pathway toward near-term quantum advantage and call for validation on real quantum hardware and larger qubit counts, making the claim speculative rather than demonstrated.
